paras: The attempted lynching of Charles Howard took place just before daylight on August 28, 1910, when a mob of about 200 men stormed the jail at Frankfort, Kentucky, intending to lynch Howard, a Black man charged with the murder of Edward Rice. The mob was turned away without injury, and the town's jailer and mayor moved Howard to the jail at Lexington. The episode drew a grand jury charge from Judge R. L. Stout, who demanded that the mob's members be brought to justice.

Howard was held in the Frankfort jail on a charge of murdering Edward Rice, whom a Frankfort dispatch described as "a white man" that Howard had shot to death. According to the same dispatch, Howard claimed he had shot in self-defense. The coverage gives no date or circumstances for the shooting of Rice.

A Lexington wire report said the jail was "stormed just before daylight" by 200 men "bent on lynching" Howard. The mob was "finally driven off without injury to any one," and Acting Governor Cox was on the verge of ordering out troops when the crowd dispersed. A Frankfort dispatch of August 30 instead described an angry mob around the jail that threatened Howard, and credited Jailer Lucas and Mayor Polsgrove with conveying him safely to the Lexington jail before harm was done. Judge Stout later told jurors that the men had come to the jail and demanded possession of a prisoner already in the hands of the law.

Mayor Polsgrove was reported to be "resolved to have no more lynchings in Frankfort." At the next session of the court at Frankfort, Judge Stout charged the grand jury to investigate the mob "without fear or favor" and to turn any guilty parties over to the petit juries. He told the jurors that but for the county officials' action a murder would have been committed "right at the doors of this courthouse," and warned that mob justice would lead to anarchy. No report of indictments of mob members or of Howard's trial was found.

Coverage came entirely from white newspapers. The Washington Times ran the Lexington wire on its front page on the day of the attack under the headline "MOB STORMS JAIL TO LYNCH NEGRO," identifying Howard by race and by the charge against him. Kentucky papers carried shorter or later items: the Paducah Evening Sun listed "Attempted lynching at Frankfort" in a column of state briefs, and the Hopkinsville Kentuckian headed its account "SAVED FROM LYNCHING By Mayor And Jailer Of Frankfort."

The Hopkinsville account was the only one to report Howard's claim of self-defense, though it stated as fact that he had shot Rice to death. The Bourbon News of Paris, Kentucky, printed Judge Stout's charge at length, including his statement that there was no bravery in joining other men "to kill a poor, cowering, trembling prisoner." No coverage of the episode in the Black press was found.

accounts.label: Lexington wire report
accounts.gist: A mob of 200 stormed the Frankfort jail before daylight to lynch Howard and was driven off without injury as the acting governor was about to call troops.

accounts.label: Frankfort dispatch
accounts.gist: An angry mob around the jail threatened Howard, who claimed self-defense in Rice's killing, but the jailer and mayor moved him to the Lexington jail before harm was done.

accounts.label: Judge's charge to the grand jury
accounts.gist: A large body of men came to the jail and demanded a prisoner; only the county officials' action prevented a murder by the mob.

framing.detail: The Washington Times ran the Lexington wire on page one under 'MOB STORMS JAIL TO LYNCH NEGRO', identifying Howard by race and the charge against him.
The Paducah Evening Sun reduced the episode to a one-line item, 'Attempted lynching at Frankfort', in its 'Kentucky Kernels' column.
The Hopkinsville Kentuckian credited the mayor and jailer under 'SAVED FROM LYNCHING' and gave Howard's self-defense claim, while stating as fact that he 'shot to death Edward Rice, a white man'.
The Bourbon News printed Judge Stout's charge denouncing men who join to kill 'a poor, cowering, trembling prisoner' and warning that mob rule meant anarchy.

versions.value: The mob stormed the jail and was driven off; it dispersed as troops were about to be called
An angry mob around the jail threatened lynching; officials removed Howard to Lexington before harm was done

conflicts.note: Not contradictory: the wire stresses the assault and dispersal, the Frankfort dispatch the removal of the prisoner. Neither gives the timing of the removal relative to the mob's withdrawal.
